Quench-Detection Pickup from Converter Ripple and Edges

§1 — Why ripple matters, and what the detectors compare

The converter ripple on the ITER coils does not threaten their insulation: a few hundred volts at hundreds of hertz is far below the partial-discharge levels. Its main safety risk is to quench detection. The detectors look for a small resistive voltage under a large inductive one, by comparing two signals that the inductive voltage drives equally. Converter ripple and switching edges divide along a winding through its capacitances, not only through its inductance. So they can drive the two compared signals unequally, and the difference appears where a quench would. If that difference reaches the threshold for the holding time, it trips a false fast discharge. If the thresholds are raised to avoid that, it blunts protection. No number for this exists in our work yet, and IDM states no immunity requirement against converter ripple or transients (PJ37K3 v1.0 PDF 4–5; 64MA7Y v1.0 PDF 20–23; Q7EFZT v1.0 PDF 4, 7–8).

The two coil families are wound differently, and their detectors differ with them. The values below were read from IDM through Lucy on 19 October 2026.

PF coilsCS modules
WindingStacked double pancakes, each wound with two conductors in hand. C1 runs from the upper double-pancake joint through the inner turn and across the inter-pancake plane; C2 starts at the pancake joint and follows the complementary path to the next joint (64MA7Y v1.0 PDF 6, 17–18)Simply wound, one conductor length per section: six hexa-pancakes and one quad-pancake, 40 layers of 14 turns, seven conductor lengths per module. Inter-pancake joints at the outer diameter, helium inlets at the inner (NENPSZ v1.1 PDF 1–2; HPYA8Y v1.0 PDF 6, 8)
What is comparedThe voltages of the two conductors in hand of each double pancake, VC1 − VC2, with the pancake joint as the bridge midpoint and a tuned weighting coefficient as the balance. Redundant sets A and B, three instrumentation wires per set per double pancake (PJ37K3 v1.0 PDF 5; 64MA7Y v1.0 PDF 13, 23; Q7EFZT v1.0 PDF 7–8, 17)Co-wound voltage taps: a QD tape inside the winding pack with two embedded stainless strips, primary and redundant. Signals are taken per double pancake (single pancake at the outermost), grouped into four sums, and compared as QI1 − QI3 and QI2 − QI4 (R3M9BQ v3.0 PDF 6, 8–11)
Filter and thresholdsA recursive exponential filter, with no numerical time constant given. The 2011 study proposed 0.1 V with holding times of 0.4–12 s; the 2024 reassessment marks those settings invalid, because the updated tap locations raise the imbalance between the conductors, and tabulates holding times per double pancake for thresholds from 0.05 to 0.5 V (64MA7Y v1.0 PDF 27–47; Q7EFZT v1.0 PDF 1, 4, 24–26)A 50 mV noise-suppression target with a 1.5 s dwell; about 300 mV for reliable detection; 500 mV with a 1.5 s hold as an example threshold. The v3.0 specification states no final setting (LYAH8Q v1.1 PDF 6–7, 20–24)
Insulation for the capacitancesHeld in the winding model: turn, pancake and ground insulation of the PF coils (coil_windings.py, εr 4)0.5 mm turn, 1 mm conductor wrap, 1 mm layer, 1 mm ground plane and 7 mm ground wrap, from a drawing marked for information only (3E6PVT v1.0 PDF 25)

Two features of the PF detection matter here. The instrumentation wire routing is part of the measured loop and can add up to 10 % to the signal (64MA7Y v1.0 PDF 18–19, 47–50). And Q7EFZT already finds the electromagnetic imbalance from the scenarios large enough that the old settings would trip a fast discharge in every pulse. Converter pickup adds to a margin that is already tight.

The turn-resolved PF winding already places both conductors in hand: coil_windings.pf_turn_layout winds the two hands side by side through both pancakes of a double pancake, joined at the outer joint (its interleaved reading, the main arm; separate is the sensitivity arm). So the PF bridge output is the difference between the two halves of each double pancake, read across the joint. The model places those turns physically, but not their capacitances: it couples each turn to the next one along the conductor, so the side-by-side hands carry none. pf-two-in-hand-capacitance places them across the insulation first, and §2 builds on that. The CS co-wound tape needs a new element: a second conductor co-located with the winding, coupled to it almost perfectly in inductance and partly in capacitance.

§2 — The PF bridge on the two-conductor turn model

A first estimate is already in the tree. qd_bridge_transfer and qd_summary in scripts/figures/iter_whole_pulse_ripple.py form each double pancake's bridge on the interleaved turn model, and the whole-pulse ripple record gives 0.26–1.04 V of peak bridge noise across the six PF coils, before any detector filter. That estimate reads one arm, drives the coil differentially only, carries 300 Hz to 2.4 kHz, and trims the bridge by subtracting its 1 Hz transfer. It stands in for the winding's losses with a loss angle at Q = 3. It also rests on a capacitance network that gives the side-by-side hands no capacitance, so this section waits on pf-two-in-hand-capacitance §2.

Move the transfer into one library owner, src/power_convertor/quench_detection.py, and widen it there:

  • It takes the turn-resolved winding from scripts/iter/exterior_turn_voltages.build_winding, which it does not rebuild, and solves the node voltages per volt at the terminals with the same nodal matrices (frequency_response_prediction.ladder_matrices).
  • It forms a detection signal as a weight vector over the nodes. The PF bridge is one set of weights: the voltage across conductor C1 minus the weighted voltage across C2, with the joint as the midpoint. The weighting coefficient is set, as the 2011 study sets it, to null the inductive signal of a slow current ramp. §4's grouped CS sums are another set of weights on the same solve.
  • The drive is differential or common mode.
  • Losses come from the installed-loss model at its low and high bounds (winding_losses, assembled as section_step_convergence._installed_losses assembles it), not from a loss angle.

The figure script is held by coil-circuit-playback-figures §9 while that runs, so its copy of the transfer is retired in §5, not here. Run the transfer for all six PF coils, from 10 Hz to 100 kHz, at both loss bounds and in both two-in-hand readings. Carry the instrumentation-wire loop as a stated assumption, up to 10 % of the signal, until its routing is known.

Done when the record gives each coil's worst double pancake and its bridge transfer at the converter lines: 300 and 600 Hz, the VS1 500 Hz carrier and its harmonics. Controls:

  • Negative: a winding with its two conductors placed symmetrically, mirror images in capacitance, gives a bridge output of zero to rounding at every frequency.
  • Negative: with every capacitance removed, the balanced bridge reads zero at the converter lines.
  • Positive: with the losses removed and the weighting coefficient at one, the differential transfer equals qd_bridge_transfer(coil, f, quality=1e12) to rounding at that script's lines, for every PF coil.

Library src/power_convertor/quench_detection.py, tests tests/test_quench_detection.py, caller scripts/iter/quench_detection_pickup.py, record docs/research/iter-quench-detection-pickup.html.

§3 — Through the detector, against the thresholds

Drive §2's transfers with the converter voltages the model already produces. The steady ripple is the switched supply's line set at each coil's worst steady operating point, read from the whole-pulse arrays in data/iter/whole_pulse_ripple/ as qd_summary reads them. The edges are the commutation steps and IGBT edges of thyristor_voltage_steps and igbt_edge_stress, carried through the same transfers in the time domain.

The detector already has an owner, ripple_margins.DetectionSection. It carries an imbalance, a common-mode rejection, an analogue bandwidth, a sampling rate, a threshold and a holding time, and pf_circuit uses it. Extend it rather than writing a second path:

  • Its imbalance may be §2's per-line bridge transfer in place of one scalar.
  • The recursive exponential filter is a first-order recursion at the sampling rate, with time constant τ, applied after sampling has aliased each line.
  • A time-domain path filters a sampled bridge signal through the same recursion and reports the longest time it stays continuously above a threshold, for the edges and for the holding-time check.

This mechanism does not depend on §2, so it is built first, as its own node. The tokamak magnet quench-detection electronics are specified in 423SYN v2.6 (approved 23 July 2026), §4.4 (PDF 35–36). The chain is a passive low-pass at −20 dB per decade with a 30 Hz cut-off, then differential amplification, then an active low-pass at −40 dB per decade with a 10 Hz cut-off, then the analogue-to-digital conversion. Sampling is not required for detection but is at least 1 kHz. That chain is the main front-end case, third order overall. The active stage's pole alignment is not stated, so a Butterworth pair is the stated assumption. It needs DetectionSection's analogue stage to take a cascade of stages. Two bounds sit beside it. One is the TF cold-test stage, a 30 Hz second-order low-pass on a 1 ms cycle (5U6PVV v2.3 PDF 12–13, 21; FYXJSN v1.0 PDF 5–6; FXW4SY v1.0 PDF 14), which tf-cold-test-validation §10 measures. The other is no analogue filter below the sampling, so that a quiet result cannot be produced by an assumed bandwidth alone. No document states τ: not Q7EFZT, 64MA7Y or 423SYN. 423SYN's noise basis assumes 300 Hz switching noise from 12-phase supplies, while the first characteristic line of a 12-pulse supply is 600 Hz; the record notes this. Carry a second sampling rate beside 1 kHz. Sweep τ from 1 ms to 1 s. Name every converter line that aliases into the filter's passband at each sampling rate: an aliased line passes the filter as if it were slow. Before the recursion, the time-domain path band-limits the signal through the same analogue stage and samples it at the detector rate. Report the filtered pickup against the thresholds from 0.05 to 0.5 V and the holding times Q7EFZT tabulates.

Done when, for each coil, each front-end case (the 423SYN chain and its two bounds), each sampling rate and each τ, the record states the largest filtered pickup in volts and as a fraction of each threshold, the double pancake that carries it, and whether it stays above a threshold for longer than the holding time. Beside it, the record gives the unfiltered bridge peak and names the converter lines that alias into the filter's passband at each sampling rate, so the reader sees what the front end removed and what passed as slow. A pickup that would trip the detector is a finding to report: how far over, at which threshold, and from which converter line or edge. It is not a defect to fit away. Negative control: with the converter ripple replaced by its averaged voltage, the filtered pickup falls to the slow electromagnetic imbalance alone, which the record states beside it. Positive controls: the existing scalar detectors in pf_circuit and tests/test_iter_pf_circuit.py give the same residuals as before; and a synthetic bridge signal at a converter line of known amplitude comes through each front-end case at its analytic attenuation, so a null pickup is shown to be the plant's and not the instrument's. For the 423SYN chain that attenuation is the product of the 30 Hz first-order stage and the 10 Hz second-order stage, so a single-stage run fails it. Detector src/power_convertor/ripple_margins.py; the PF results extend §2's caller and record.

§4 — The CS co-wound tape

Add the co-wound stainless tape to the sectioned CS winding as a second conductor that follows the winding through every pancake: coupled to it almost perfectly in inductance, and capacitively through the turn insulation that 3E6PVT draws. The tape is a winding element, so it goes in coil_windings beside the CS layout. Build it for any sectioned winding, with CS as its first instance. tf-cold-test-validation builds no tape element and only measures. Validating the element against its TF07 and TF17 converter-to-tape transfers needs a sectioned TF winding, which does not exist yet. That winding, the element's TF instance and the comparison with the measurements go to a separate plan, tf-co-wound-tape-validation. This section closes on the CS instance, and its pickup is reported as not yet validated against a measurement. The tape's capacitive pickup is not a static divider. The strip is a continuous conductor read end to end at high impedance, so its capacitive contribution is displacement current flowing along the strip times the strip's impedance. That contribution vanishes as the frequency falls and approaches the divider only where the strip is electrically long. Model the strip as a distributed RC line along each pancake. Take its series resistance from the strip's material and section where IDM gives them. Otherwise bound it, taking as a cross-check the 4–5 kΩ that the CS module site acceptance test, 3JUPSH v3.1 (PDF 20–22), reads from each co-wound-tape tap to the conductor. That reading also means the strip is referenced to the conductor through kilo-ohms rather than left floating. Restate the ripple, insertion and slow-imbalance results on that model. Three controls test the mechanism itself:

  • At zero frequency the capacitive contribution is zero to solver precision, which the static divider fails: it reads 4.96e-4 V/V at 1e-6 Hz.
  • Below its corner, the capacitive contribution rises in proportion to frequency, and doubling the strip's series resistance halves the corner frequency.
  • In the limit of a long strip, ωrcℓ² ≫ 1, the weights reproduce the static divider's.

Form the four grouped sums and the comparisons QI1 − QI3 and QI2 − QI4 as R3M9BQ v3.0 defines them, as weight vectors on §2's solve in quench_detection. Then drive them as §3 does and filter them through §3's detector. The drive is CS1's switched ripple, with the circulating band coil-circuit-playback-figures §9 restores to the CS arrays, and its switching-network insertion front. Where the tape's dimensions or its exact place in the turn are not in IDM, state the assumption and run both ends of its range. The winding carries §6's coupling secondary as §2's solve does, using CS's conductor coupling where IDM states it and otherwise §6's stated analogy, run from k2 = 0.80, the TF analogy, to 1.00, coupling with no loss.

Done when the record gives the filtered comparison pickup against the 50 mV noise target and the 300–500 mV thresholds with the 1.5 s hold, for the ripple, for the insertion front and for the slow imbalance the window's mean voltage drives, at each of §3's front-end cases, both sampling rates, across its τ range and at k2 = 0.80 and 1.00, beside the unfiltered comparison peak, and names the pancake group that carries the worst of it. Negative control: a tape with no capacitance to the winding, coupled inductively at unit coupling, gives zero comparison pickup at the converter lines, to the solver's precision. At the tape's stated coupling, the comparison pickup falls to the residue of the coupling's shortfall, which the record states beside the capacitive result. Caller scripts/iter/cs_quench_tape_pickup.py, record docs/research/iter-cs-quench-tape-pickup.html.

§6 — The coupling secondary on the whole winding

§3's first results node, pf-detector-pickup, recorded its edge results in the §3 tables of the pickup record and in its evidence anchor pf-detector-pickup of the landing record. Those results crossed the trigger §2 set. With the conductor-coupling term as modelled, a held converter edge reaches 0.26 V on PF2 behind a 30 Hz second-order stage and stays beyond 0.05 V for 3.7 s. The capacitive floor stays below 5 mV, and the same holds in all six coils (16,316 of 22,512 edge cases). The term is one passive secondary per winding (k2 = 0.80, τ2 = 0.49 s). But winding_losses.mechanism_conductance reflects it as branch conductances, one per section from that section's self-inductance. The bridge balances against the full inductance matrix, mutuals included, so a held step leaves a slow imbalance that is the representation, not the winding.

A secondary that links each section's flux reflects an impedance proportional to that flux, so in the frequency domain the whole inductance matrix carries one factor, Leff(ω) = L·(1 − k2·jωτ2/(1 + jωτ2)), on every self and mutual term alike. Use that form in quench_detection's node solve, and expose it from winding_losses beside the branch form, so that one owner holds the coupling parameters. The time-domain studies stamp the losses as resistors and cannot take a frequency-dependent factor, so they keep the branch form; the record says so. Regenerate the bridge data.

Done when, with the coupling term on, PF6's main-reading bridge transfer equals, to rounding, the lossless bridge of the same winding with its inductance scaled by f(ω); its 10 Hz value falls from 1.5e-4 V/V to no more than the coupling-off capacitive floor; every coil's bridge data are regenerated; and the record states the change and its scope. The two transfers are not expected to be equal with the coupling term on and off, because above 1/τ2 the factor tends to 1 − k2 and the capacitive imbalance scales with the effective inductance. The record also flags that k2 = 0.80 is the TF cold-test analogy carried to PF, which puts the PF effective inductance near 20 % of nominal above about 0.3 Hz. That is a stated assumption whose consequence is now material. Negative control: the branch form restored reproduces §2's 1.5e-4 V/V at 10 Hz on PF6. Positive control: with capacitances removed, the bridge reads zero at every frequency with the coupling term on. Library src/power_convertor/winding_losses.py and src/power_convertor/quench_detection.py, tests tests/test_quench_detection.py and tests/test_winding_losses.py, caller scripts/iter/quench_detection_pickup.py, record docs/research/iter-quench-detection-pickup.html. §3 holds a node on each side of this section: its first results node supplied this section's premise, and its final results node, the 423SYN chain at every case, follows this section.

§7 — A per-line accessor on the detector

ripple_margins.DetectionSection.residual() folds each converter line onto its alias at the sampling rate. It applies the analogue stages to each line at that line's own frequency before sampling, and the recursion at the alias the line folds onto. It then sums the lines that share an alias into that alias, as complex amplitudes. A caller that needs each line's own filtered amplitude recomposes it by hand. tf-cold-test-validation §12's margins caller does so, and its per-line sums match residual() to 1e-12 only where no two lines collide. This plan's scripts/iter/quench_detection_pickup.py recomposes lines too.

Add a public method to DetectionSection that returns each alias's filtered amplitude, keyed by alias frequency and naming the converter lines folded into it. Express residual() through it, so that one path computes both. Move this plan's caller onto the accessor. tf-cold-test-validation's caller is that plan's: tell its coordinator when the accessor lands, and do not edit its script from here.

Done when the following hold:

  • tests/test_detection_section.py checks the accessor against an independent hand computation of a case built so that two converter lines of known amplitude and phase fold onto one alias. The expected alias amplitude is the magnitude of the complex sum of each line through its own analogue response and the recursion at the alias. A second case has no collision.
  • The existing scalar residuals in pf_circuit and tests/test_iter_pf_circuit.py are unchanged, bit for bit.
  • Every caller in this plan reads the accessor rather than recomposing lines: scripts/iter/quench_detection_pickup.py and any figure script under scripts/figures/ that composes detector lines.

Negative control: an accessor that adds the colliding lines' magnitudes instead of their complex amplitudes fails the hand-computed collision case.
